title: First exchange
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: annyeonghaseyo is the whole greeting system. One word, any hour, anybody — there is no morning, afternoon or evening version to choose between, and it is used both for meeting somebody and for arriving somewhere.

A yes/no question is made with the VOICE and nothing else. The words do not move, no word is inserted, and the ending does not change: haksaeng-ieyo is 'is a student' and haksaeng-ieyo? is 'is a student?'. There is no equivalent of English 'do', and nothing is turned around the way it is in German or French.

ne and aniyo answer the QUESTION, not the fact. ne means 'what you said is right', so if you are asked haksaeng-i anieyo? ('aren't you a student?') then ne means 'right — I am not'. English answers the fact and would say 'no' there. This one takes real practice to hear.

Korean has two goodbyes and the choice is about who moves. annyeonghi gaseyo is said to the person LEAVING; annyeonghi gyeseyo to the person STAYING. Both mean 'go / stay in peace', and getting them the wrong way round is the most common visitor's slip in the language.

An answer leaves out everything both of you already know. Ne, haksaeng-ieyo is a complete reply with no subject at all — putting one in would be like answering 'Is he a student?' with 'Yes, he is a student, that student, the one we are talking about'.

jal jinaeseyo? is not the automatic second half of a greeting the way 'how are you' is in English. It asks a real question and expects a real answer, and it is for somebody you have not seen for a while. Say it to the same shopkeeper every morning and you will sound odd.

The -se- sitting inside jinaeseyo, gaseyo and gyeseyo raises the person the sentence is about, not the person you are talking to. That is why you ask jal jinaeseyo? and answer jal jinaeyo without it: you lift the other person, never yourself.

gamsahamnida and mannaseo bangapseumnida end in -mnida, which belongs to a more formal style than the -yo this course speaks. They are kept because they are what is actually said at a first meeting and when thanking a stranger. Learn them whole; the style they come from is a later level's work.

words.note: 'Hello' — the only one you need, at any hour, with anyone. A question in origin ('are you at peace?'), which is why it ends like one. The bare annyeong is for friends and is not taught here.

sentences.trap: There is no time-of-day greeting to reach for. A learner who goes looking for 'good morning' will find that Korean simply does not divide the day up this way.
sentences.sound: an-nyung-ha-SE-yo, five even beats. The ny in the middle is one sound, as in English 'canyon'. Nothing is stressed — an English speaker will want to lean on the last syllable, and flattening that out is most of what makes it sound right.

variations.changed: a name after a comma, exactly as in English

variations.cue: Hello. It has been a long time.
variations.changed: the greeting plus the line that often follows it
the greeting and the question, in the order they come

mistake.why: Split in two, annyeong is the casual hello friends say to each other and haseyo is a bare verb with nothing to do. The greeting is one word; the space changes what you have said.

sentences.usage: Meeting anyone, at any hour, in any place.

words.note: 'Well'. It goes in front of the verb it describes, which is where Korean puts every adverb — and since the verb is at the end, jal is usually the second-to-last word in the sentence.
'To be doing'. jinaeyo is about yourself; jinaeseyo carries the -se- that raises the person asked about. So you ask jal jinaeseyo? and answer jal jinaeyo — lifting yourself would be strange.

sentences.trap: This is not the English reflex 'how are you'. It is a real question about how life has been going, and it is asked of somebody you have not seen for a while — not of the person who serves you coffee every day.
sentences.sound: jal ji-nae-SE-yo, and the voice RISES on the last syllable. That rise is the only thing making this a question, so it has to be real: say the same words flat and you have told somebody they are doing well.

variations.changed: the answer — the raised -se- comes out, because you do not lift yourself
about somebody else, and still no rise at the end
said flat it is not a question at all — it is a wish, and a normal way to part

mistake.why: Something has been added to build the question, and there was nothing to build. Korean question-making is done entirely by the voice at this level; a syllable stuck on the end is a word that does not exist.

sentences.usage: Meeting somebody you have not seen for weeks or months.
sentences.mnemonic: The question mark is in your voice, not in the sentence.

words.note: 'Yes' — read it as 'that is right'. It agrees with the question asked, not the fact underneath, so after a negative question ne means 'right, it is not'. English does the opposite.
'Well'. It goes in front of the verb it describes, which is where Korean puts every adverb — and since the verb is at the end, jal is usually the second-to-last word in the sentence.
'To be doing'. jinaeyo is about yourself; jinaeseyo carries the -se- that raises the person asked about. So you ask jal jinaeseyo? and answer jal jinaeyo — lifting yourself would be strange.

sentences.trap: Nothing here says 'I'. The answer to a question about you is simply the verb, and adding jeo-neun would push the sentence towards 'as for ME, I'm fine' — a contrast nobody asked for.
sentences.sound: ne, jal ji-NAE-yo. ne is short and light, closer to English 'neh' than to 'nay'. The whole answer falls at the end, which is what tells the listener it is an answer and not another question.

variations.changed: the same words handed back, with the raised -se- and a rise, to return the question
the other answer — and a hint of the 'cannot' that a later level teaches properly
the reply that closes the exchange rather than continuing it

mistake.why: The subject has been put in twice, once at each end, which is what happens when you translate word by word and then check yourself. Korean drops it entirely: the answer is the verb.

sentences.usage: Replying when somebody asks how you have been.
sentences.mnemonic: Answer with the verb; everything else is already understood.

words.note: A man's given name, and here it is the topic of a question. A name is asked about exactly as any other noun is: put the topic marker on it and let the intonation do the questioning.
'Student', from the last module. In a question the word does not change at all — haksaeng-ieyo is both 'is a student' and 'is a student?', and only the voice tells them apart.

sentences.trap: Nothing moves. In English the question turns the sentence around — 'Minsu is' becomes 'is Minsu' — and in German the verb jumps to the front. Korean does neither, and a learner who reorders the words has written a sentence that no longer parses.
sentences.sound: MIN-soo-nun HAK-ssaeng-ee-eh-yo, with the whole last syllable lifting. Everything before the rise is said exactly as the statement was said in the last module — which is the point.

variations.changed: a different person under the same question
a different guess, and -yeyo after the vowel
the same words said flat — a statement again

mistake.why: The verb has been dragged to the front the way English and German build a question. Korean questions leave the sentence exactly where it was.

sentences.usage: Checking something you half know about somebody.

words.note: 'Yes' — read it as 'that is right'. It agrees with the question asked, not the fact underneath, so after a negative question ne means 'right, it is not'. English does the opposite.
'Student', from the last module. In a question the word does not change at all — haksaeng-ieyo is both 'is a student' and 'is a student?', and only the voice tells them apart.

sentences.trap: The reply has no word for 'he'. English cannot leave the subject out and so reaches for a pronoun; Korean leaves out what is obvious, and reaching for a pronoun here is the clearest sign of an English speaker.
sentences.sound: ne, HAK-ssaeng-ee-eh-yo, falling at the end. The k of haksaeng tenses the s that follows it into a double ss — that is automatic in Korean and it is why this course spells the word the way it does.

variations.changed: a different answer to a different question

variations.cue: No, he is not a student.
variations.changed: the denial, with -i on the noun and anieyo at the end
an answer that adds something instead of repeating the question

mistake.why: A word for 'he' has been supplied. It exists, and it is used in writing, but in a spoken answer like this it lands as heavy and pointed — as if you were distinguishing him from somebody else.

sentences.usage: Confirming what somebody has just asked.
sentences.mnemonic: If they already know who, do not say who.

words.note: 'No' — again, read it as 'that is not right'. It contradicts the question. It is a relative of anieyo ('is not') from the last module, and the family resemblance is real: both are about denying.
'Doctor', from the last module, answering the question this time. Notice that the answer says only uisa-yeyo — no subject at all, because everybody already knows who is being talked about.

sentences.trap: aniyo denies the QUESTION. Asked 'is Minsu a student?', it says 'that is not right', and then the sentence supplies what is right. It is not the English 'no' attached to a fact.
sentences.sound: a-ni-YO, oo-ee-sa-YEH-yo. aniyo has three light beats and no stress; the ui of uisa is that quick oo-to-ee slide again, and it rewards being said slowly until it settles.

variations.changed: the same denial with the other answer behind it

variations.cue: No, my friend is a doctor.
variations.changed: the correction says who, because this time it is not obvious
the same answer after agreement instead of denial

mistake.why: The marker has been dropped from uisa. A denial needs -ga on the thing being denied — uisa-ga anieyo — and without it the two words sit side by side with nothing joining them.

sentences.mnemonic: First say the guess was wrong, then say what is right.

sentences.cue: It has been a long time.

words.cue: it has been a long time
words.note: 'It has been a while' — for someone not seen for months. Its end is -ieyo, the copula you know, on a noun meaning 'a long interval': Korean says 'it is a long interval'.

sentences.trap: English says 'long time no see' and puts the seeing in it. Korean says only that a long interval IS — no seeing, no you, no me. Look for a verb of meeting in it and you will not find one.
sentences.sound: o-raen-ma-NEE-eh-yo. The n at the end of oraenman links straight into the -ieyo, so the join is heard as ma-ni-e-yo — the same running-together that happens every time a word ending in a consonant takes this ending.

variations.cue: Hello. It has been a long time.
variations.changed: the pair as they are actually said, greeting first

variations.cue: It has been a long time. Are you well?
variations.changed: and this is where jal jinaeseyo? properly belongs

variations.cue: Has it been a long time?
variations.changed: the same words with a rise — asking rather than saying

mistake.why: The ending has been cut off. What is left is the bare noun, which is what close friends say to each other; in the style this course speaks the sentence needs its -ieyo.

sentences.mnemonic: It is not 'long time no see' — it is 'it is a long while'.

words.note: 'Pleased to meet you', learned whole. The -mnida ending is the formal style of a meeting or a stage, kept because it is exactly what a first introduction says. Take it as one move.

sentences.trap: Do not take this apart to translate it. The first word means 'having met' and the second 'I am glad', and the whole thing is a set move at a first introduction — the sort of phrase you learn as one gesture rather than as grammar.
sentences.sound: man-na-SUH ban-gap-sseum-ni-da. It is long, and it is meant to be: the length is part of the courtesy. The p in bangapseumnida turns into an m before the n that follows, so it comes out ban-gam-seum-ni-da when said quickly.

variations.changed: the full opening of a first meeting, both halves

variations.cue: Pleased to meet you. My name is Minsu.
variations.changed: the phrase and then the introduction it makes room for
the same phrase handed back after somebody else has said it

mistake.why: Two politeness styles have been stacked on one phrase. The -mnida ending is already the formal one; adding -yo on top of it is like signing a letter twice. Say the phrase exactly as it is, or say nothing after it.

sentences.usage: Said once, at a first introduction, and not again.
sentences.mnemonic: One gesture, one phrase, learned whole.

words.note: 'Thank you' — the other frozen -mnida phrase, for a stranger, a shopkeeper or a colleague. There is a warmer -yo-style thanks too; this is the safe one to start with.

sentences.trap: This ends in -mnida, not -yo, and that is deliberate. It is the polite thank-you a stranger expects; the -yo version exists and is warmer, and warmth with a stranger is the thing a learner cannot yet judge.
sentences.sound: gam-sa-HAM-ni-da. The h in the middle is barely there — most speakers say gam-sa-am-ni-da at speed. As always, no syllable is stressed, and the phrase is said as one even run.

variations.changed: accepting something and thanking for it in one breath
how you leave a shop — you are the one going, so they are the ones staying
the two phrases that will carry a whole first day

mistake.why: The ending has been cut off, leaving the bare noun 'gratitude'. It is not a word anybody says on its own — the thanks lives in the ending, and without it you have named a feeling rather than expressed one.

sentences.usage: Thanking anyone you are not close to, which at this stage is everyone.
sentences.mnemonic: The long one is the safe one.

words.note: 'Peacefully' — the word that starts both goodbyes. On its own it is never said; it waits for the verb that follows it, exactly as jal does.
Two verbs, one row — the Korean goodbye: gaseyo 'go', gyeseyo 'stay'. annyeonghi gaseyo to whoever is LEAVING, annyeonghi gyeseyo to whoever STAYS. Both carry the respectful -se- of jinaeseyo.

sentences.trap: There are two goodbyes and this is only one of them. Say it to somebody who is staying put and you have told them to leave — which is why the pair has to be learned together, as one decision about who is moving.
sentences.sound: an-nyung-hee GA-se-yo. The first word is the greeting's first two syllables plus -hi, which is a real family resemblance and worth noticing. gaseyo carries the same raised -se- as jinaeseyo.

variations.changed: the other one — said to whoever is staying, so this is what you say on your way out of a shop
the parting agreed and returned
the two-line close of almost any transaction

mistake.why: Said by a customer on the way out of a shop, this is the wrong half of the pair: the shopkeeper is staying, so it has to be annyeonghi gyeseyo. The sentence is perfect Korean and the situation is wrong, which is the harder kind of mistake to notice.

sentences.usage: Parting from somebody who is leaving while you stay.
sentences.mnemonic: Whoever moves gets gaseyo; whoever stays gets gyeseyo.

comprehensionPool.cue: Yes, I am well. Thank you.
It has been a long time. Hello.
Pleased to meet you. My name is Yuna.
No, she is not a doctor.
